opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an important milestone, though I'd frame it carefully, because "novel scientific discovery" covers a lot of ground.

What makes AlphaEvolve significant is that it's a general-purpose system. Our earlier work, like AlphaFold or AlphaTensor, was built for a specific problem. AlphaEvolve combines the creativity of large language models, in this case Gemini, with automated evaluators inside an evolutionary loop. The model proposes changes to code, the evaluator rigorously checks whether they're actually better, and the best candidates are refined over many generations. That combination matters. Language models on their own can hallucinate. But if you ground them in something that can verify correctness, you can use their creativity to search spaces humans have struggled to explore.

The results showed it isn't just rediscovering known things. In matrix multiplication, it found a way to multiply four-by-four complex-valued matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's 1969 algorithm in that setting. That's a problem people have worked on for more than fifty years. We applied it to over fifty open problems in mathematics. In most cases it matched the state of the art, and in roughly a fifth of them it improved on it, including a new lower bound for the kissing number problem in eleven dimensions.

What excites me just as much is that the same system was useful in practice. It found a scheduling heuristic for Google's data centers that recovers a meaningful fraction of our worldwide compute. It also sped up kernels used in training Gemini itself. So in a small way, the model is helping make its own training more efficient.

Now, the caveats. AlphaEvolve works best where you can write down a clear, automatable evaluation function: where "better" is something you can measure. A lot of science isn't like that yet. Forming hypotheses, designing the right experiment, or deciding which question is worth asking are still very human activities. So I wouldn't say we've built an AI scientist. I'd say we've shown that for a broad class of problems, AI can be a real partner in discovery, producing results that are new, verifiable, and that experts find interesting.

The bigger lesson for me is about the method. The discoveries came from pairing generative models with rigorous verification, and from collaboration with mathematicians and engineers who knew which problems mattered. I think that's the template for how AI will accelerate science: amplifying scientists by letting them explore much larger spaces of ideas than they could alone.

r001.rationale: It describes Gemini proposing code changes within an evaluator-driven evolutionary loop and says the system found a new matrix multiplication algorithm.

r002.rationale: It says the evaluator rigorously checks candidates and reports a new lower bound for the kissing number problem, presenting a new, verifiable mathematical result from the system.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely important milestone, but I want to be precise about what kind of milestone it is, because it's easy to overclaim in both directions.

The thing that made AlphaEvolve different from a lot of what came before is that it wasn't just solving a problem we already knew how to solve, faster or at larger scale. It actually improved on results that very smart people had been stuck on for a long time. The matrix multiplication result is the one people tend to cite, where it found a way to multiply four-by-four complex matrices in forty-eight scalar multiplications instead of forty-nine, which is a bound that had stood since Strassen in 1969. And then across a collection of open mathematical problems, in a meaningful fraction of them it either matched the best known constructions or improved on them. Those are not toy problems. Those are problems that mathematicians had put real effort into.

So I think the significance is that it demonstrated that a system built around a general-purpose language model, combined with an evolutionary search loop and an automated evaluator, can produce artifacts that are new to human knowledge. Not new to the model, not a rediscovery, but new to the field.

Now, the honest caveats. The problems it works well on share a particular structure: you can write down a function that scores a candidate solution automatically and reliably. That's true for a lot of algorithm design and combinatorial constructions, and it's true for things like data center scheduling or kernel optimization, which is where we got some very practical wins inside Google. It is not yet true for most of science, where the evaluation is an experiment in the physical world or a judgment call about whether an idea is interesting. So I wouldn't say AlphaEvolve is a system that does science in general. I'd say it's an existence proof that the discovery part, the creative search for something that didn't exist before, is no longer off-limits to AI in domains where verification is cheap.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that it worked best as a collaboration. The mathematicians chose the problems, framed what a good solution looked like, and interpreted what came back. In several cases the construction the system found gave people a new idea about why the problem behaved the way it did. That human-in-the-loop pattern is, I think, the realistic near-term shape of AI in scientific discovery, and AlphaEvolve is the clearest early example of it actually working.

So, a milestone, yes. The first time I felt comfortable saying an AI system had contributed something novel to mathematics in a way that would survive scrutiny. But the frontier now is extending that to domains where you can't just run the evaluator a million times, and that's a much harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a general-purpose language model combined with an evolutionary search loop and automated evaluator produced novel mathematical artifacts, including a new matrix-multiplication algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response describes novel constructions and improved results, but does not state that the system can prove new mathematical results.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an important milestone because it shows how AI can move beyond answering questions to proposing ideas, testing them, and improving them. In science, having a plausible idea is only the beginning. The crucial question is whether it actually works.

What makes this approach powerful is the feedback loop: generate a candidate solution, evaluate it, and use that evidence to guide the next attempt. When you can evaluate candidates reliably, you have a way to search for discoveries that may not be obvious to a human.

But I would distinguish that from having an autonomous scientist. Choosing a meaningful problem, deciding what counts as progress, and understanding why a result matters remain essential. So I see AlphaEvolve as a step toward AI becoming a much more active partner in discovery, with its creativity grounded in results we can check.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI generating and evaluating candidate solutions, but does not state that a large language model coupled with a harness can discover new algorithms.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that a large language model coupled with a harness can prove new mathematical results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what makes AlphaEvolve significant is the move from solving a problem once to participating in an iterative process of discovery. You propose an idea, test it, get feedback, and use that feedback to produce a better idea. That loop is central to scientific work.

The key question is whether the system can produce something genuinely new and whether we can establish that it works. In mathematics and computer science, you can sometimes build very precise evaluators, so a surprising proposal can be checked rather than simply accepted because it sounds convincing. That combination of creativity and verification is particularly powerful.

I would distinguish that from saying we now have an autonomous scientist. Choosing the right problem, deciding what matters, and understanding the implications of a result remain substantial challenges. But I see AlphaEvolve as an important step toward AI becoming an active contributor to discovery, helping us explore possibilities we might otherwise never have considered.
